title: Rock a named midget fuse out of its open-clip block with a tong puller
instruction: The control panel is de-energized and its door is open. Pick up the yellow fuse puller from its holder beside the enclosure, reach into the enclosure and grip fuse F2 (CONTROL XFMR, the fuse with the orange label) across its body in the puller's jaws, holding the puller perpendicular to the fuse, tip the puller's handles away from you to lever the near end of the fuse out of its clip first, then lift out the far end, and drop the fuse in the blue parts tray beside the enclosure. Do not disturb fuses F1 and F3 or the wiring.
context: Pulling cartridge fuses is regular work for electricians (SOC 47-2111) and industrial maintenance workers (49-9071, 49-9041): when troubleshooting a control panel they isolate it, open its door, remove a suspect fuse to test or replace it, and put the circuit back in service. The fuse sits in an installed panel: inside the enclosure's walls, on a DIN rail between wire ducts, with wires landed on both of its terminals. On open-clip midget fuse blocks it is taken out with an insulated tong puller, and because the spring clips grip hard it is rocked out one end at a time: pulled straight, the puller slips off or the fuse jerks free and flies. Taking the wrong fuse cuts power to a circuit that is still needed (here the PLC supply or the cabinet light), so finding the named fuse and leaving its neighbours and the wiring alone is part of the job. A robot that can do this frees a qualified worker from a frequent, repetitive step of panel maintenance.
setup: Positions are measured forward from the line joining the two arm bases (61 cm apart), left or right of their midline as seen from behind the robot, and up from the table top. Enclosure: a Rittal AE 1036.500 wall-mount steel enclosure (300 x 300 x 155 mm outside, 1.4 mm walls, grey RAL 7035, one hinged door) lies on its back on the table, opening up and its bottom (gland plate) end toward the robot, spanning 17 to 47 cm in front of the bases and from 11 cm right to 19 cm left of the midline; its rim is 15.5 cm above the table, with a 12 mm lip round the opening. Its door, hinged along the left wall's rim, stands open at 100 degrees (just past upright, toward the left). Inside, its 254 x 275 mm mounting plate (top 2.05 cm above the table) carries a 35 mm DIN rail running left-right 32 cm in front of the bases, and two slotted grey wire ducts (38 mm wide, 51 mm tall) parallel to it, centred 20.9 cm and 43.4 cm in front of the bases. Fuse blocks: three Eaton Bussmann BM6031B one-pole midget fuse blocks (black, 76.2 x 21.0 x 30.7 mm; two tinned-copper spring clips 26.4 mm apart; a box lug at each end) sit on the rail side by side, 1.5 mm apart, their long axes pointing away from the robot and their centres 32.0 cm in front of the bases: F1 2.25 cm left of the midline, F2 on the midline, F3 2.25 cm right. Each holds a 10 x 38 mm midget fuse (Bussmann KTK class: 10.3 mm nickel-plated ferrules, fibre tube, 9 g) with its axis 5.3 cm above the table. Wiring: each block has a black 14 AWG line wire from its far lug straight into the far duct and a red 14 AWG load wire from its near lug straight into the near duct, 4.4 cm above the table. Labels: a 34 x 20 mm circuit label on the far duct's cover above each block: 'F1 PLC 24V DC' on white, 'F2 CONTROL XFMR' on orange, 'F3 CABINET LIGHT' on green. Puller: an Ideal 34-015 one-piece yellow nylon tong fuse puller (127 mm; two flat arms joined by a loop at the handle end, notched handles next to the loop, curved jaws at the tips whose grooves run across the tool; jaws sprung open) stands upright, jaws down and arms parting left-right, in the 2 cm deep pocket of a grey holder block (4 x 5.6 cm, 6 cm tall) on the table right of the enclosure, 31.0 cm in front of the bases and 17.5 cm right of the midline. It is used perpendicular to the fuse: pointing down into the block, its jaws close across the fuse body from either side between the clips, where the block's walls are cut down. Tray: a blue parts tray (10 x 10 cm inside, 2.5 cm walls) on the table right of the enclosure, centred 20.0 cm in front of the bases and 20.0 cm right of the midline. Both arms start at the ready pose with their grippers open. One fixed layout, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Milestones: 0.25 the puller is picked up (moved 2 cm or more from where it stood in its holder); 0.5 then its jaws are closed across F2's body between the ferrules; 0.75 then F2 is out of both clips (each ferrule's centre 7 mm or more from its clip's centre, so the circuit is open) while held in the puller's jaws; 1.0 then F2 lies at rest inside the tray's walls. Cap: if F2 comes out of both clips at any moment without the puller's jaws on it (before 0.75 is reached), the score can be no more than 0.5 for the rest of the trial, even if the puller grips it afterwards and it ends in the tray. Hazard: the score is 0 for the whole trial, from the moment F1 or F3 moves in its clips (its centre 2 mm or more from where it sat, or tilted 4 degrees or more), even if milestones were already reached or are reached afterwards. Otherwise the score is the highest milestone reached. A reviewer checks positions with a rule, and from the video that F2 was in the jaws when it left its clips.
run_limit: 3,000 steps (150 s at 20 Hz); the scripted demo finishes in 1,388 steps (69 s)
reset_notes: Press F2 back into its two clips (both ferrules seated, the label end toward the robot) and check that F1 and F3 are fully seated and that every wire is still landed in its lug and in its duct. Stand the puller back in its holder beside the enclosure, jaws down, arms parting left-right, empty the tray and leave the door open at about 100 degrees. About 1 minute.
fidelity: PhysX 480 Hz, rigid bodies, the station's i2rt arm gains. Clip fingers: fixed faces 0.7 mm inside the ferrule (BMM603 STEP) with a compliant-contact spring (60 kN/m, friction 0.4): about 70 N to pull a fuse straight, 33 N at one end (real force unpublished). Puller jaw shape, flex and opening inferred; notched handles grip 0.8, smooth arms 0.25. Enclosure, door, ducts and wires are rigid fixed colliders (wires do not flex); plate standoff inferred. Details in README.
